the fort holds a lot of history, but sadly, there’s no information inside to educate visitors about it. there isn’t much to explore within the fort itself - you simply stroll around, enjoy the elevated views, and take pictures. the city of port louis looks stunning from up here, offering great photo opportunities of both the city and the fort. entry is free, and you can park your car right outside before heading in.

the fortifications de québec national historic site is one of the most significant pieces of québec city’s history. walk through the gates and upon the ramparts and take in the gorgeous views of old québec. the only fortified city north of mexico, one cannot visit québec city without admiring the fortified walls and ramparts which were the city’s defensive system built between 1608 and 1871. today, the fortifications of québec consist of 4 gates, 3 martello towers, the citadelle, and 4.6 km of ramparts, complete with cannons, which encircle old québec’s upper town. in the more than 300 years of its history, québec has come to possess a variety of fortifications, all of which can be explored on an hour-long circular walk. the bastions, walls, towers, gates, and countless old cannons show how well the former french colony was protected. the four and a half kilometers of defensive ramparts on the west flank of the old city were constructed of granite and sand, the only fortifications of this kind in north america. numerous pieces of weaponry are a constant reminder of québec's troubled past. there are 4 gates in this fortification (enter /exit from upper quebec) 1. st. jean gate 2. kent gate 3. prescott gate 4. st louis gate

the fortress is massive and so well-preserved. you can really imagine what life was like when soldiers were stationed here hundreds of years ago. the views of the ocean are absolutely stunning - bring your camera! i could have spent hours just taking photos from the different levels. there are so many rooms, tunnels and lookout spots to explore. the staff was friendly and they have these little exhibits explaining the history. i had no idea the fort was attacked so many times throughout history! if you're in san juan, this is absolutely a must-see. give yourself at least 2 hours to really explore it properly.

the forum of trajan is one of the most impressive ancient spaces in rome with a scale that still surprises. the massive columns the wide open layout and the famous trajan’s column tell a story of ambition and empire. even in ruins the site feels alive full of texture history and quiet strength. you can walk around the edges take in the details and imagine the grandeur it once held. at sunset the stones glow with soft light and the whole area takes on a calm timeless beauty. it is a must see for anyone who wants to feel rome’s true weight.

the französischer dom (french cathedral) stands proudly on berlin’s gendarmenmarkt and is one of the square’s architectural highlights. despite the name, the "dom" refers to the tower and not to an actual cathedral in a religious sense. the church itself was originally built by the french huguenot community in the early 18th century, who had fled persecution in france and settled in berlin under the protection of prussian kings. the current tower was added later, in 1785, and today it serves as an observation platform and museum. visitors can climb to the top for panoramic views over gendarmenmarkt and central berlin. the museum inside the tower is dedicated to the history of the huguenots and their influence on berlin’s culture and economy. the inscription on the building — added during the 1905 renovation — reads: “to the glory of god, for the blessing of the community, under the protection of the hohenzollerns.” architecturally, the structure reflects neoclassical and baroque elements, with its distinctive dome and statues. whether you're interested in religious history, french-german relations, or simply enjoying beautiful architecture, the französischer dom is a must-see in berlin

the free range peacocks (and other birds) were so cute! the place is also very quiet, and calming. definitely a great way to escape one of the busiest areas of prague.

the freely accessible garden in the inner block of palazzo venezia is an excellent place for a short rest during a walking tour of rome, especially on hot summer days. you will also find a drinking fountain here. the star of the garden is the fountain from 1730, symbolizing the venice's marriage to the sea. all this is hidden in the shade of palm trees, magnolias and other types of plants and flowers. and since this place is a bit out of the way, there is no overcrowding of tourists.

the french market place is not to missed. yes it's full of "tourists" but it's also full of the best people watching in the city! fabulous hat shops, jewelry, and a zillion things you didn't even know you needed!! food & drink everywhere. we needed lunch and ac, both were found at the market cafe! jazz played, and a terrific meal (huge portions). little park-like settings intertwined amongst the shops. have fun, meet the vendors, and take in the best of the quarter!

the french market was an excellent place to visit while visiting new orleans. it was loaded with fascinating items, food, and flea market delights. there was food and a band playing; there was overhead covering so it was comfortable to walk in during the heat, and there was a dining area and a bar. i would highly suggest visiting when you go to new orleans.

the french quarter has lots of places to eat, drink, and smoke. the higher rated restaurants need reservations, and some are booked a week out. lafayette cemetery is closed for repairs . the other popular ones require you to be part of a tour. the french quarter at night, it is very busy and crowded, but earlier in the day, it's not bad. parking can be hard to find, but we always found a place after driving around a bit. the places with music tend to be loud, so you can't talk. all in all, i think nola is a bit overrated, but it's an interesting place to visit for two or three days. posted reviews for individual places and tours separately.

the gardens of la tropical are the paradigm of modernist landscape architecture in cuba and constitute a jewel of art nouveau architecture nestled in the green lung of the city. with an area of ​​297,154 m2, they were designed by the catalan master builder who emigrated to cuba at the beginning of the century, ramón magriñá, who left the imprint of spanish organic gardens on them. they were located on the banks of the almendares river, close to the factory land in puentes grandes, a developing industrial neighborhood, to which it provided a valuable natural space. in 1904, the park was inaugurated with three halls: the ensueño hall, mamoncillo and la cúpula, hence, at that time, the vegetation practically absorbed most of the areas, leaving little surface free of plants and trees. with all intention, the master builder let architecture and nature merge into a single landscape, intertwined to the point of confusing the real with the artificial. to do this, he used gray cement, elevating its decorative possibilities to the maximum expression, an unprecedented feat in cuban architecture. at the same time, magriñá respected the orography of the land and practiced the art of toparia in some bushes, close to the rest areas. he cultivated timber, fruit and medicinal species. one of the main dance halls was built around a century-old mamoncillo tree, from which it took its name. as a modernist garden it had several caves designed mainly in ferrocement. one of the most amazing features of this venue is the exquisite use of this material in the recreation of railings, picnic areas, canteens, benches and lounges that reproduce authentic tree trunks or rock surfaces in their shape and texture. the connection achieved between these objects made by the artist and the natural elements is extreme. the decorative structures are integrated into the natural space, intersecting with it and creating a pleasant space where everything seems to be the work of nature. in this sense, its modernist conception transcends the garden's own landscape layout, to take care of the detailed imitation of the naturalistic environment in the decorative and architectural elements themselves." water was another natural element used by magriñá for the design of the park, given the proximity to the almendares river. in the first half of the 20th century, a new building and several outdoor recreational spaces were added to the gardens, such as a gym area, a tennis court, and a skating court. however, the insertion of these new architectural elements did not alter the original design of the park and the preeminence of the green space. of the same profession and a countryman of the main teacher, the architect jaime cruanyas feliú, collaborated with magriñá in the buildings carried out in the gardens between 1906 and 1914. of these, the most important was the castle, erected in 1911, and conceived as a gambling house and residence of the local administrator. its splendid decoration evokes the style of the imposing buildings of the alhambra in granada and the mosque of córdoba. after the construction of the la tropical gardens in havana, new recreational spaces were established that also included a landscape design. this is how the polar gardens, the cotorra gardens, the havana forest, the zoological garden, among others, emerged. there are similarities between the la tropical gardens and the emblematic park güell, the work of the famous master antonio gaudí, especially between the ensueño room in the havana park and the hypostyle room in the barcelona garden. in los jardines de la tropical, which is more than a hundred years old, you can still see, dimly, the glamor of other times.

the gardens of palazzo venezia are a quiet corner of history in the heart of rome. built in 1455 by cardinal pietro barbo, who became pope paul ii, the palazzo was one of the first renaissance buildings in the city. designed by francesco del borgo, it marked a shift from medieval fortifications to the harmony and balance of the renaissance. the palazzo served as a papal residence and later housed the venetian embassy, from which it takes its name. it witnessed critical moments in history, from renaissance diplomacy to mussolini’s speeches from its iconic balcony in the 20th century. today, it houses a museum, but its gardens remain an often-overlooked treasure. surrounded by arcades and dotted with classical statues, the gardens feature a central fountain and carefully maintained greenery. once a retreat for cardinals and diplomats, they now offer a glimpse of renaissance aesthetics and design. if you visit, take a moment to sit by the fountain—it’s not just a garden but a space shaped by centuries of history, quietly preserved in the middle of the city. this place is an incredible hidden and quite spot to relax and escape from the noisy piazza venezia.

the gardens of rijksmuseum are a nice place to sit and chill. there are fountains, statues, flowers, and a coffee shop. there are, also, loads of chairs so you will find somewhere to relax. the gardens are on each of the four corners of the museum. it's not worth a special visit, but if you happen to be passing or have just visited the museum, then it is worth popping in.

the gardens, paths, and structures surrounding the meiji jingu shrine are absolutely beautiful, and honestly some of the best public spaces in the city of tokyo in my opinion. it’s more densely forested and enjoyable than the gardens surrounding the imperial palace, and it’s more well-kept than some of the other public parks in shibuya and shinjuku. i loved walking through the paths, looking at the impressive architecture, archways, and the austere design on the primary shrine in the center of the gardens. it’s a very peaceful and relaxing place, and is large enough that you can get some decent exercise by walking about in the park. if you want to visit public parks in tokyo, this one should be at the top of your list.

the gayer-anderson museum is an art museum situated adjacent to the mosque of ahmad ibn tulun. the building takes its name from major robert grenville gayer-anderson pasha, who resided in the house between 1935 and 1942 with special permission from the egyptian government. the museum is noted for being one of examples of 17th-century domestic architecture left in cairo, and also for its collection of furniture, carpets, curio, and other objects. also known as bayt al-kritliyya is considered to be one of the remarkable examples of muslim domestic architecture in cairo. it dates back to the mamluk period (1040 ah/1631 ad) and it was built by hagg mohamed salem galmam el- gazzar. it later came into the possession of a wealthy muslim woman from crete, and the home became popularly known as beit al-kritliyya, or "house of the cretan woman. the second house, to the west (the innermost side in relation to the mosque) was built in 1540 ad (947 ah) by abdel-qader al-haddad. it later became known as "beit amna bint salim, after its last owner. the two houses were joined by a bridge at the third floor level at an unknown point, and are both collectively known as bayt al-kritliyya. in 1928 the egyptian government began to clear the homes, many of which were in very poor condition, away from the mosque as part of a plan to make important islamic monuments more accessible. the committee for the conservation of arab monuments objected to the demolition of bayt al-kritliyya, however, on the grounds that the home was well preserved. the home was kept intact, and repairs were made to the side walls to strengthen them after the neighboring houses were torn down. in 1935, major gayer-anderson, a retired collector and self-described orientalist, was granted permission to reside in the house, which had just been restored. gayer-anderson oversaw the installation of electricity and plumbing, and the restoration of fountains, pavements, and other parts of the interior of the home. he populated the building with his personal collection of art, furnishings, and carpets, and he built a sailing boat he used to collect these antiques from all over egypt, it was docked on the gayer-anderson museum is an art museum situated adjacent to the mosque of ahmad ibn tulun. the building takes its name from major robert grenville gayer-anderson pasha, who resided in the house between 1935 and 1942 with special permission from the egyptian government. the museum is noted for being one of examples of 17th-century domestic architecture left in cairo, and also for its collection of furniture, carpets, curio, and other objects. also known as bayt al-kritliyya is considered to be one of the remarkable examples of muslim domestic architecture in cairo. it dates back to the mamluk period (1040 ah/1631 ad) and it was built by hagg mohamed salem galmam el- gazzar. it later came into the possession of a wealthy muslim woman from crete, and the home became popularly known as beit al-kritliyya, or "house of the cretan woman. the second house, to the west (the innermost side in relation to the mosque) was built in 1540 ad (947 ah) by abdel-qader al-haddad. it later became known as "beit amna bint salim, after its last owner. the two houses were joined by a bridge at the third floor level at an unknown point, and are both collectively known as bayt al-kritliyya. in 1928 the egyptian government began to clear the homes, many of which were in very poor condition, away from the mosque as part of a plan to make important islamic monuments more accessible. the committee for the conservation of arab monuments objected to the demolition of bayt al-kritliyya, however, on the grounds that the home was well preserved. the home was kept intact, and repairs were made to the side walls to strengthen them after the neighboring houses were torn down. in 1935, major gayer-anderson, a retired collector and self-described orientalist, was granted permission to reside in the house, which had just been restored. gayer-anderson oversaw the installation of electricity and plumbing, and the restoration of fountains, pavements, and other parts of the interior of the gran plataforma of tulum: a monument to maya ingenuity in the heart of the ancient walled city of tulum, mexico, stands a structure of great historical significance: the gran plataforma (great platform). this imposing stone foundation is more than just a piece of architecture; it is a testament to the ingenuity and cultural sophistication of the maya civilization that once thrived along the yucatán peninsula’s coast. the gran plataforma served as the foundation for several important buildings within the ancient city of tulum. as the city’s name, which means "wall" in yucatec maya, suggests, tulum was a fortified port city that played a crucial role in the maya’s trade network. the gran plataforma elevated key structures, such as temples and administrative buildings, providing them with a strategic advantage—both in terms of defense and visibility. positioned on this elevated platform, these buildings would have been visible from the sea, signaling tulum’s power and importance to incoming traders and visitors. the gran plataforma itself is a marvel of maya engineering. built from large limestone blocks, the platform is an example of the maya’s advanced construction techniques and their deep understanding of the local environment. the structure’s design reflects the maya’s ability to adapt their architecture to the coastal landscape, ensuring the stability and durability of their buildings despite the challenges posed by the region’s tropical climate. the buildings that once stood atop the gran plataforma were likely centers of religious, political, and economic activity. temples dedicated to the gods would have played a central role in the spiritual life of tulum’s inhabitants, where priests conducted rituals to honor deities and seek their favor. these religious activities were deeply intertwined with the city’s governance and trade, reinforcing the maya belief in the divine right of their leaders and the sacredness of their city. the platform’s prominence within tulum also symbolized the city’s connection to the broader maya world. tulum was a key node in the extensive trade network that spanned the yucatán peninsula, connecting it to other powerful maya cities like chichen itza and coba. the goods that passed through tulum—such as obsidian, jade, textiles, and cacao—helped sustain the city’s economy and influence. the gran plataforma served as a physical reminder of tulum’s role in this complex web of commerce and culture. today, the gran plataforma stands as a silent witness to the rise and fall of tulum. as visitors walk among its ruins, they can imagine the bustling activity that once took place atop this great platform—the prayers of the priests, the decisions of the rulers, and the exchange of goods that connected tulum to the rest of the maya world. though the structures that once crowned the gran plataforma have long since fallen, the platform itself endures, a symbol of the resilience and ingenuity of the maya civilization. the gran plataforma in tulum is not just a remnant of an ancient city; it is a monument to the architectural and cultural achievements of the maya. its enduring presence offers a glimpse into the past, reminding us of the sophisticated society that once thrived along the coast of the yucatán peninsula. for those who visit tulum, the gran plataforma is a powerful link to the history, spirituality, and ingenuity of the maya people.

the grand canyon national park is a breathtaking natural wonder that exceeded my expectations in every way. the vast expanse of the canyon is awe-inspiring, with its intricate layers of rock and stunning vistas. hiking down into the canyon was a thrilling experience, with the scenery changing dramatically as i descended. the colorado river, which carved out the canyon over millions of years, is a powerful force that commands respect. the park's scenic drives, such as desert view drive, offer stunning views of the canyon from various angles. watching the sunset over the canyon was a highlight of my trip, with the colors of the rocks and sky changing in a mesmerizing display. the park's visitor centers and museums provided valuable insights into the geology, history, and wildlife of the area. the south rim is well-developed for tourism, with plenty of amenities and activities available. however, it's still possible to find quiet spots and enjoy the peacefulness of the park. overall, the grand canyon national park is a must-see destination for anyone who loves nature and the outdoors. whether you're hiking, camping, or just taking in the views, the grand canyon is an unforgettable experience.

the grande montagne nature reserve offers a captivating journey into a world of rare flora and fauna. this verdant sanctuary stands as a testament to the island's unwavering commitment to conservation. as you step onto the winding trails, you're immediately enveloped by the sights and sounds of a unique ecosystem. the air is rich with the scent of wild herbs and alive with the calls of endemic birds found nowhere else on earth. your guide, a fountain of knowledge and humor, effortlessly switches between french and english, peppering the tour with fascinating facts and playful quizzes that keep everyone engaged. plant enthusiasts will marvel at the botanical treasures, including the near-mythical café marron, a species brought back from the brink of extinction. wildlife encounters abound, from the colorful rodrigues fody soaring overhead to the gentle aldabra giant tortoises ambling along the paths. as you ascend, the forest occasionally parts to reveal breathtaking panoramas of the island and the vast indian ocean. what truly sets grande montagne apart is its tangible commitment to environmental stewardship. the meticulously maintained trails, and the ongoing research projects all speak to a profound respect for nature. whether you're a seasoned naturalist or simply someone who appreciates unspoiled wilderness, the grande montagne nature reserve offers an unforgettable experience. it's more than just a tourist attraction; it's a living classroom that inspires a deeper connection with the natural world. as you plan your rodrigues adventure, make this ecological gem a priority – it's a journey that will linger in your memory long after you've left the island's shores.

the great pyramid of giza, also known as the pyramid of khufu or cheops, is the largest and oldest of the three pyramids on the giza plateau near cairo, egypt. built during the fourth dynasty around 2600 bce, it originally stood at about 146 meters tall and remained the tallest man-made structure in the world for more than 3,800 years. today, after erosion and the loss of its smooth outer casing, it stands at about 138 meters. constructed as the tomb of pharaoh khufu, the pyramid is a masterpiece of ancient engineering. it is estimated to contain around 2.3 million limestone blocks, each weighing between 2.5 and 15 tons. the precision with which these blocks were placed continues to astonish scholars and engineers, as does the scale of the workforce and logistics required. inside, the pyramid has a complex interior design, including the king’s chamber, queen’s chamber, and the grand gallery. despite centuries of study, mysteries remain about how it was built and the full meaning of its design, inspiring countless theories and research. the great pyramid, a unesco world heritage site and one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, is standing as an enduring symbol of ancient egypt’s architectural and cultural achievements.

the high line is an absolute gem that new york should never lose. just the idea of revitalizing an old railway into a public green space is brilliant—it’s a shining example of creative urban renewal. this raised walkway offers a truly unique way to experience the city. a great place to walk in new york, the high line runs above the streets of manhattan’s west side, providing fantastic views of the bustling neighborhoods below. there’s so much to see along the way—lush plants and trees, striking sculptures, and ever-changing art installations. i even saw a huge pigeon sculpture that really stood out! originally constructed in the 1930s, the high line was part of the west side improvement project. it served as an elevated freight rail line, removing train traffic from dangerous street-level routes. for decades, it carried goods directly into warehouses and factories. after falling into disuse in the 1980s, the line was nearly demolished. fortunately, a grassroots group called friends of the high line fought to preserve and repurpose it. their efforts paid off when the first section opened to the public in 2009. now, the high line is not just a park—it's a piece of living history, a cultural destination, and a perfect place to walk, relax, and take in the unique character of new york city.

the high line is an incredible blend of nature, art, and architecture in the heart of manhattan. walking along the elevated path, you get amazing views of the city and hudson river while surrounded by beautifully maintained gardens. there are plenty of benches to relax, and the atmosphere feels calm despite being in the middle of new york. a must visit spot for both locals and tourists.

the highest peak in mauritius and at the same time probably the easiest to climb. if you can't find a parking right at the entrance (which bears not a lot of space for parking) just go on about 300m inlands along the road to the gorges viewpoint. here is enough parking available. as said the trail is quite easy, only when it rained or has rained a lot it can be very deep and muddy. be prepared to dive your feet ankle deep or bit more in the mud. in about 1.5 hrs you can be on the peak. only the end of the trail up to the peak is to be done on all fours and can be, owing to the loose soil, a bit slippery. but the view is amazing. between april and july you might find some guavas along the way, a nice vitamin reward. also bringing along an ice cold blue marlin is an amazing reward after the hike. if you like to have it more difficult and want to go the whole nine yards (828m), then start from the bottom of the valley in the gorges (drive to the visitor center parking down in the valley). check on wikilogs for a route because there are no signs put up for this route. i saw a route which went further than the peak along the black river ridge trail down to cascavelle. maybe you can tell your driver to wait there if you want to conquer it. but be prepared for a hard trail.

the highest peak of south korea. (the highest peak of the korean peninsula is located at north korea) the mountain is call halla-san, and the volcanic cone located on the top of it is called baekrokdam, which means white deer's lake. you can find a sign says 白鹿潭(baekrokdam) here, where 99.9% of people takes selfies. there is a wooden deck next to it, where you can sit and relax. however, it doesn't block winds. the lake usually doesn't have much water. the only time you can see the full lake is during summer, which is very cloudy so that you may not see the lake at all. during winter, snow covers the lake. there are 5 hiking courses in the hallasan, but only two can reach baekrokdam. the gwaneumsa course, which is located on the north face of the hallasan, is the steepest one. however, is considered the most beautiful course, since you can see the samgakbong, and the northern wall. the gwaneumsa course has only one bus every hour, which only goes to the jeju national university. if you are trying to go to the jeju city, you'll have to transfer to the other buses at the jeju national university. the sungpanak course is the course located at the east face of the hallasan. the course starts with a 4km path which has merely no elevation. there is a oreum call sara in the middle of the course, where you can see the hallasan's reflection on a lake. however, besides that there aren't many things to see since the whole course goes through a forest. there is a closing time at every rest area for safety.

the highlight of my may 2025 trip to yellowstone was finally getting to see and experience the colors of grand prismatic spring from the grand prismatic spring overlook. over the years i've made numerous attempts all of which failed for one reason or another. if you go too early, and there's no wind, the steam masks the formation. if you go to late, you can't find a parking spot. if there's bear activity, they close the trail. when you do make it up and get the chance to look down at the grand prismatic spring from the overlook, you see a riot of fiery oranges, golden yellows, deep reds, and brilliant turquoises, appearing almost supernaturally vivid against the soft, falling snow. it was like the earth itself was exhaling beauty, and i was lucky enough to be there to inhale it! standing on the overlook, enveloped by a gentle snowfall, felt like i was witnessing a sacred, living, and breathing masterpiece of nature. the falling snow added a layer of magic, making the already vibrant colors of the grand prismatic spring feel even more alive, a true testament to the raw, untamed artistry of nature. the bright, vivid colors in the spring are the result of "microbial mats of thermophilic bacteria" around the edges of the formation. the mats produce colors ranging from green to red; the amount of color in the microbial mats "depends on the ratio of chlorophyll to carotenoids and on the temperature gradient in the runoff." in the summer, the mats tend to be orange and red, whereas in the winter the mats are usually dark green. the center of the pool is sterile due to extreme heat: 188.6 degrees in the center of the pool.

the hike from skeleton point to the tipoff was, without a doubt, one of the most beautiful hikes i have ever been on. the views in this section of the park are absolutely incredible and take your breath away. unfortunately, you're gonna need your breath if you decide to hike here, because although the hike down isn't too bad, what comes down must also come back up, and the way back up is orders of magnitude harder. hiking here is not for the casual hiker or people who aren't in great shape. getting here requires a round-tip hike of nearly 9 miles, nearly all of which is hills. doing this hike, even if you are a fast hiker, will take you at least 5 hours. and make no mistake, if you come this far, your only options to get out are climbing back up the 3,200+ feet of elevation you climbed down, or being evacuated on a helicopter. if you have doubts about your ability to handle this hike, don't do it. there is a reason why the nps recommends you stop at skeleton point if you are doing this as a day hike. and if you are in good enough shape to hike here, make sure you bring plenty of water, because you aren't going to find any on the trail. that said, if you are up for the challenge and are fit enough to handle it, this section of the trail is, in my opinion, the most beautiful section, hands down. once you get to the tipoff, you have a really difficult decision: turn around and hike the minimum 3 hour, 4.5 miles uphill back to the trailhead, or continue another 2 miles downhill to the colorado river and the bright angel campground. i hiked all the way to the campground, and then back up the bright angel trail, and completed the nearly 17 mile hike in 8 hours and 17 minutes. so doing it in a day is possible, but i would not recommend this unless you are a very experienced hiker in really good shape. if you want to do this section, seriously consider making it a two-day hike and camping in the bright angel campground at the bottom of the canyon. regardless of how you try and tackle this hike, the views in this section are worth it

the imperial carriage museum in vienna is a fascinating journey through austria’s regal past, offering visitors an extraordinary glimpse into the opulence and grandeur of imperial life. nestled within the grounds of schönbrunn palace, this museum houses an impressive collection of carriages, sleighs, and ceremonial vehicles that once belonged to the habsburg dynasty. from the moment you step inside, the atmosphere is one of reverence and awe, transporting you to an era of imperial splendor. one of the highlights of the museum is the iconic coronation carriage, an extravagant masterpiece that showcases the pinnacle of craftsmanship and design. its intricate gold details, rich velvet upholstery, and symbolic motifs leave no doubt about its role in royal pageantry. the surrounding exhibits, which include children’s carriages and funeral hearses, provide a comprehensive perspective on the life cycle of the monarchy, making the experience both informative and emotionally evocative. the museum’s layout is thoughtfully curated, with chronological and thematic displays that are easy to follow. informative plaques in multiple languages, as well as an optional audio guide, offer rich historical context. each carriage is presented in a way that highlights not only its aesthetic appeal but also its historical significance. visitors are encouraged to take their time exploring, as there is much to absorb in the finer details of each artifact. beyond the carriages themselves, the museum offers insight into the lives of the people behind these opulent vehicles. exhibits include personal items belonging to empress elisabeth (sisi) and emperor franz joseph, adding a deeply human dimension to the experience. these personal touches make the grandeur of the carriages feel even more poignant, as they remind us of the individuals who once occupied these magnificent vehicles.

the imperial citadel of thang long is a unesco world heritage site and one of hanoi’s most historically significant landmarks. walking through its gates, you can feel the layers of history — from ancient dynasties to more recent wartime structures. the main gate, doan mon, and the flag tower are especially impressive, offering great photo opportunities and a real sense of the capital’s royal past. the site covers a large area with archaeological remains, exhibition rooms, and peaceful gardens. i particularly enjoyed the displays of ancient artifacts and the old stone foundations that reveal the citadel’s scale and importance. however, some sections could be better maintained, and a few exhibition areas felt a bit sparse or lacking detailed explanations in english. on hot days, there’s not much shade, so it can be tiring to explore the entire site without breaks. that said, the citadel is still a must-visit for history lovers, and with a bit more curation and preservation work, it could easily become one of the most engaging historical attractions in southeast asia.

the imposing structure of the national capitol of cuba is located in central havana, and the architecture of the building is truly stunning. it can be visited if arranged in advance, but even if you don't go inside, you can admire the beauty of the place.

the inca stairs lead to the top of the isla del sol. at the top, there is a terrific panoramic view of the island and the beautiful lake titicaca. the stairs dated back to 15th century ad and are a little steep but manageable for one of average fitness. the stairs also lead to yumani village

the incredible scenes from this place will remain deeply etched in our memory. one of the places where you can see natural beauty in all its glory. children, like us adults, are delighted and full of impressions from this magical place. i thought tickets were expensive, but this is worth every penny

the indian astronomical observatory (iao) in hanle, ladakh, is one of the highest and most fascinating observatories in the world. situated at an altitude of over 4,500 meters, it offers crystal-clear skies, making it a perfect destination for astronomy lovers and curious travelers alike. a visit to the iao is not just about stargazing—it’s a chance to experience india’s cutting-edge space research up close. the observatory is managed by the indian institute of astrophysics and plays a crucial role in space studies, including tracking stars, galaxies, and cosmic events. the view of the night sky here is breathtaking. with minimal light pollution and high altitude, visitors can see thousands of stars, constellations, and even the milky way with the naked eye. it’s an unforgettable experience, especially for children and students interested in science. access is limited since it’s a high-security and sensitive area, so plan your visit in advance and check for permits. even if you can’t enter the main observatory, the surrounding area itself offers an incredible astronomical experience. for anyone traveling to ladakh, hanle’s indian astronomical observatory is a must-see for its unique blend of science, nature, and wonder.

the infrastructure of the park is neglected and the buildings seem to be abandoned. there are several picnic areas with city or beach views. a paved road leads to the favela. there is also a path leading to the wall under the mountain of dois irmanos. this is not a path to the top, but if you are a mountain hiking enthusiast, this trail is for you - several places with a nice view, exotic vegetation and no tourists. to enter the path, you need the help of a local map or an app with 'all trails' trails

the international park is a peaceful and refreshing place, perfect for families, kids, or anyone looking to relax and enjoy nature. it offers plenty of green space, clean walking paths, and shaded areas for sitting. the environment is calm, and the air feels fresh—great for a morning walk or evening visit. you will find some playgrounds and seating areas that are well maintained. while it may not have many food or drink options, it's still a lovely escape from the busy city life. i highly recommend it for a quiet day out or a casual gathering with friends and family. excellent place. i loved it during the evening. this review reflects my personal experience and opinion only.

the ironic thing about this part of australia being so infamous for the great barrier reef is the mangrove swamps that span the entire coast from the marina to up north west of the township. they had to build a swimming pool with artificial sand to mimic a true beach. i guess this place survives simply based on the draw of the reefs and the tourism that comes with it.

the is an excellent short but strenuous hike that gets you to the top of the first stage of the sugarloaf gondola ride. it's about 220m up i believe and can be done in 40min up and 20min down, i estimate. important. the gate at the top closes at 17:00. so while the bars and cafés are open, you're only option up after 17:00 is paying the gondola. same on coming down after 17:00. the gate at the bottom where you enter the park from urca closes at 18:00. so the intention is to get people coming down by 17:00 so that when the sun sets, people aren't stuck under the thick dark forest canopy.
the island is a bit old-fashioned in terms of buildings, but it is brightly colored thanks to the shop windows.

the island is a wonderful place for birds and many other species. the guide was also really good and was explaining well what they are doing to protect the birds and maintain the ecosystem. but this island is also a paradise for mosquitoes. thousands of them will follow you around. be prepared and wear long sleeves shirt and a leggings if you do not want to be annoyed by them. even mosquito repellent was not enough for our group. an alternative will be to visit aride for the same fauna and flora experience without mosquitoes.

the island is beautiful and the water is incredible. the residents drive too fast and kill a lot of birds. there are so many unneutred stray dogs and cats which are known to kill many endangered species yet nobody does anything about it. along with that there is a real problem with litter and keeping up the town. the other islands are better organized, cleaner with fewer stray dogs and cats, so it can be done. the expectation is that these islands are kept clean and the endangered species are kept safe.

the island is home to around 200 aldabra giant tortoises that roam freely, making every visit feel like a wildlife encounter in paradise. seeing them up close, especially the 127-year-old elder among them, is something truly special. the island also has a lovely mangrove boardwalk and some stunning beaches, all surrounded by crystal-clear waters. it’s peaceful, not crowded, and perfect for nature lovers. a must-visit if you’re in the area!

the island is really beautiful but i can't shake off the feeling that it's beautiful only to look at. the only activity on this island i found wholesome is diving and animal watching, because there is huge amount of marine life, and i highly recommend it. snorkeling is definitely a good idea too. vegetation-wise it's basically no different from other places in brazil. the beaches are visually stunning and it's indeed pretty easy to find a spot just for yourself, but they are not that great to relax due to the lack of bars with normal prices or even places where you can resist the waves, wind and airborne sand. once you see handful of beaches and make that obligatory sunset photo, the beaches start to look the same. the sun is really aggressive so i found the best strategy is to find a palm tree or rock and hide in it's shade for most of the time. transportation is a chapter on its own. there are places where one has to needlessly walk around a whole neighborhood to reach a beach or anything really. one can rent a buggy but i felt like what this island needs less is more tourists on buggies. bikes aren't a great option due to the heat. taxis are very expensive if used regularly and buses go sometimes in unforseen intervals and are unusable if you lack cash. which happened to me and i found it absolutely impossible to withdraw cash on this island on sunday, which is a shame for such a touristy place. prices are soo high here for almost everything. 1.5l water bottle for 12 reais is not an exception in groceries. restaurants overpriced, serving mediocre food. i recommend tapiocaria de archipelago which serves great food and drinks for decent prices. the preservation tax, which was 370 reais for 4 nights is high, but still understandable, is made worse by the 358 reais entry fee for the ever present national park. the latter was too much for me so we avoided entering it. if you go diving, i recommend maravista or other agency that offers diving away from the park, because most do it inside and then you have to pay the enter fee anyway. all in all fernando de noronha is a place that's good to see at least once, but is overpriced and its services are lackluster.

the island of santa cristina is located in the northern lagoon, not far from torcello and the northern coast. in 1986 it was acquired by the swarovski family. with careful restoration of the buildings and horticultural areas, the production of a native wine called ammiana was started, a name derived from the islands of costanziaca and ammiana, whose names are not even mentioned on the topographic map. born as a roman port, these islands hosted people who escaped the barbarian raids, they exhausted their historical function in the late middle ages, sinking into the dark waters and disappearing from the light of the sun and from the memory of many. only archaeologists and underwater researchers would be able to search the bottom of the canals for the faint signs of the ancient existence. it is still surrounded by an ancient salt mine, a precious commodity for the trade of the serenissima venice.

the island serves as venice’s main cemetery, with separate sections for catholic, orthodox, and protestant burials. in 1807, under a napoleonic decree banning burials within the city, the island was officially designated as venice’s cemetery. originally, the site consisted of two separate islands—san michele and san cristoforo—but these were joined between 1835 and 1839 by filling in the canal between them. the church of san michele, designed by mauro codussi in 1469, is considered one of the earliest examples of renaissance architecture in venice. next to the church once stood a monastic complex, parts of which are still preserved today.

the isolated nature of this beach makes it an ideal destination for individuals in search of a tranquil escape from the bustling crowds of white beach. the immaculate white sandy shores and clear waters of secret beach create a breathtaking scene. what distinguishes this beach from the rest on the island are the magnificent rock formations scattered along the coastline, enhancing its intrinsic beauty and establishing it as the most visually stunning beach on boracay island.

the jaffa flea market is a treasure trove of nostalgia and culinary delights. the friendly merchants add to the vibrant atmosphere, making the experience even more enjoyable. exploring the market feels like stepping back in time, with its unique vintage items and charming shops. and let's not forget the mouthwatering israeli culinary treats that can be found there. a visit to the jaffa flea market is an absolute must!

the janela do inferno hike is an absolute must for adventurers on são miguel! with stunning views and some unexpected highlights, this trail will have you questioning whether you're hiking in paradise or sneaking a peek into the underworld. highly recommend!

the japan national stadium in tokyo is a striking venue with great energy during the football match. however, the seats were cramped, and people were hesitant to move for us to pass. food sold out quickly, leaving little available at halftime, and there was no draft beer service at the seats like at baseball games. the team store was inconveniently located, requiring a long walk to buy merchandise—adding one per floor would help.

the jasper information centre is an absolute treasure and the perfect starting point for any adventure in jasper national park. housed in a beautifully preserved heritage building right in the heart of town, the centre offers not only practical information but a warm, welcoming atmosphere that immediately makes you feel connected to the spirit of the rockies. the staff here are phenomenal—knowledgeable, friendly, and truly passionate about the area. whether you’re planning a multi-day hike, looking for hidden gem viewpoints, or just trying to figure out where to spot wildlife, they go above and beyond to help you tailor your visit. their insider tips made our trip unforgettable. beyond the helpful advice, the building itself is worth a visit. the rustic stone-and-log architecture is iconic, and there's a real sense of history in its walls. there are informative displays about the park’s geology, wildlife, and history, which make it a great little stop even on a rainy day. we left with detailed maps, new hiking ideas, and a deeper appreciation for jasper. this place sets the tone for everything that makes the park so special—nature, heritage, and warm canadian hospitality. don’t miss it—your jasper experience will be so much better if you start here.

the jeju folk village is an interesting display of a centuries-past jeju village, complete with the island's famous black pigs. while it does offer an audio guide for each section, the english version is really hard to listen to as it sounds like it's both a direct ai translation and computer voice narration. a tour would be recommended to make the history come alive because without an effective audio guide or animated live guide, one can begin to lose some interest after awhile as it is very large. we really loved the camellia maze and the beautiful gardens throughout. allow yourself some time. unlike other places we visited, this was not packed wall to wall with tour groups. maybe we were lucky.

the jesuit stairs are one of dubrovnik’s most iconic landmarks, famously featured in the “walk of shame” scene from game of thrones. while the spot tends to be quite crowded — especially during peak hours — it’s definitely worth a visit for both fans of the series and history lovers alike. the architecture is beautiful, and the stairs open up to a charming square at the top. once you reach the top, don’t miss kopun, a fantastic restaurant just a few steps away. the food is excellent, the setting is peaceful despite the tourist buzz, and it’s a perfect reward after the climb. right next to it, you’ll also find st. ignatius church, a stunning baroque church that adds to the beauty and serenity of the area. whether you’re exploring dubrovnik for its cinematic fame or its cultural depth, the jesuit stairs are a must-see — just try to go early in the morning or late in the evening to avoid the crowds!

the jewish quarter has better design than the islamic quarter in front of it, but it has been neglected greatly. in fact, they have been neglected together and have become very different due to the random renovation of its residents. however, these countries are trying to return it to its original state, although it is impossible to return 100% of it.

the jia curated exhibition going on there right now is one of the best installations i have seen . the way the exhibitors blend in the abundant space with street tags around is amazing . not to miss this exhibition if you are in bali .

the joan miro exhibition is showing from mar-july 2025. cost is 2300 yen, but two of the galleries are free of charge (not miro). well worth a 2-3hr visit! also, there’s a special bonus seeing cherry blossoms in ueno park!

the joan miró foundation is a bit far from the city center, but it’s absolutely worth the trip. the building itself is beautiful, the architecture is inspiring, and the collection of miró’s works is truly impressive. there’s also a fun interactive space where you can try your hand at creating something yourself, and the terrace offers a stunning view over barcelona. i really recommend it, especially if you love art and want a different perspective on the city.

the joan of arc garden is one of the jewels of the plains of abraham and owes its name to the equestrian statue of joan of arc that stands in its center. the garden has its special style: rectangular and built slightly below ground level, it combines the french classical style with the british-style beds. visitors have an opportunity to admire over 150 species of annuals, bulbs, and, especially, perennials. this garden is within the plains of abraham (national battlefields park). accessible free of charge, the garden is unveiled at dusk with a lighting system that varies according to the atmospheric elements thanks to the system connected to the quebec city weather station.

the journey to black glacier is very interesting. of the 90 some kms journey, 48 kms were on a rough, gravelled road. if you drive yourself (and not tour bus), there are several spots on the way that are out of a picture book. several images below are from spots on the way. the black glacier in itself is not as interesting. it is a glacier that is covered with dirt a d debris and hence black. but the surrounding mountains and the lake beneath the glacier is magnificent

the journey to lipton’s seat isn’t easy steep, winding roads test your patience but the reward is pure magic! endless emerald tea plantations stretch to the horizon, with misty valleys painting a dreamlike scene. sunrise or sunset, the view is surreal. pro tip: wear comfy shoes, go early to avoid clouds, and savor a fresh cuppa at the viewpoint. worth every bump on the road

the jozani national park is a great tourist attraction. there's a guide who takes you on a walking trail in the forest. two distinct species of monkeys are seen here. there's a mangrove forest worth visiting. all in all a satisfying experience

the jurong lake gardens are split in three sections and each one is absolutely breath taking. the interspersed greens and waters truly bring out the beauty of this place. i also appreciated the multiple spots to sit, relax, eat and for public convenience. there's a lot of walking to do but i highly recommend visiting. you'll not regret it!

the kallur lighthouse is among the most visited attractions in the breathtaking faroe islands. located on the long and narrow kalsoy island, the views you get here are otherworldly. you can reach it via ferry from klaksvik. the small white and red painted lighthouse is nestled on the northernmost tip of the kalsoy island. everyone wanting to visit the scenery will go for a hike. kallur lighthouse was built in 1927 and is now steadily growing in popularity. the lighthouse sits on the northernmost point of kalsoy island. when in the faroe islands, you need absolutely to set aside a full day for this attraction. in order to reach the lighthouse, you will need to take a short ferry ride (20 minutes) from klaksvik in the bordoy island, drive through 4 narrow tunnels and eventually hike for an hour. kalsoy island is surrounded entirely by the north atlantic ocean. the only way to get to the island is by jumping on the small kalsoy island ferry (the ferry is called sam) that departs from the town of klaksvík on borðoy island. from kallur lightghouse you can see the northernmost parts of the islands of kunoy, vidoy on eastern side and eysturoy on the western side. once you reach kalsoy island, make your way north passing through narrow four tunnels along the way. in the end, you will reach the most northernly settlement on the island, trøllanes. it will cost you 200 dkk per adult to hike to the lighthouse but it's well worth it. all hikes to the public lighthouse start from trøllanes. the hike from the trøllanes to kallur lighthouse takes one hour each way. the hike to the lighthouse is moderate in difficulty. initially, the hike is a bit steep without being scaring at all. then you will walk along the sheep path until you reach the scenery where the lighthouse is located. most people will find the hike fairly easy. the scenery you get at the end of the hike is worth every minute of the effort. expect mud on the path along the route to the lighthouse. the kayak tour for sunrise over the xochimilco fields, canals and mountains was truly magical! the best thing you could do at 3 in the morning 😄 dress warm and bring a towel to keep your butt dry and book the extra breakfast option to enjoy a great meal with coffee/coco bread, fruits and a hearty portion of chilaquiles. we had a group of really fun people and frida was an amazing guide! she made sure everybody was always feeling great and also told us a lot about the nature and the axolotls living in the waters. when sunrise came we were at a portion of the canal with optimal view and she made sure everybody had a good spot. after breakfast one of the kayak guides even hopped in an axolotl costume for a birthday celebration 😂 it was an amazing day/night and i can just recommend it to everybody

the kayaking experience was incredible! paddling through the fjords offers a unique perspective of the landscape. our guide, teresa, was fantastic providing us with many facts about the area. the group we were with was very friendly, which made the experience even more enjoyable.

the kbal spean is a hindu temple nestled up on this mountain. you need to have a valid angkor ticket for access. carvings of hindu gods on the rocks where the river runs , these echoes hinduism influence in cambodia. warning ...it is a hike to get there ! you will be walking in jungle weather, it can get really hot and humid. such rewarding waterfalls at the top . our local guide said u can bathe in the waterfall.

the khue van cac was built in 1805 and is one of five gates that divide the inner area of quoc tu giam into five different spaces. khue van cac is considered a symbol of vietnamese culture and in 1997, khue van cac was officially named the symbol of the capital of hanoi. designed in the traditional vietnamese architectural style, khue van cac has four square pillars with elaborate patterns on the ground floor and is open on all four sides. there are four round windows on four sides of the red attic. the roof is made up of two overlapping roofs, top and bottom. the more you look closely, the more unique and attractive confucian architecture attracts your attention. after passing khuê văn các, a large square well spreads out in front of you, and on the left and right are altars of 72 people who were once the greatest disciples of confucius.

the koko crater arch trail is a hidden gem for those seeking a short but challenging hike with breathtaking views. the trail is relatively steep, with some rocky sections that require careful footing, but the payoff is worth it. the arch itself is stunning, and the panoramic views of the coastline and surrounding landscape are simply spectacular. parking: the parking situation is manageable but can fill up quickly, especially during peak hours. arriving early in the morning is recommended to secure a spot. trail details: the trail is not well-marked, so it’s important to stay aware of your surroundings and follow the path carefully. the incline is steep, and there are some narrow spots, so it’s not ideal for beginners or those with mobility issues. experience: the hike to the arch and back can be done in about 1-2 hours, depending on your pace. the final approach to the arch involves some scrambling, but it’s a rewarding experience for those who enjoy a bit of adventure. tips: bring plenty of water, wear sturdy shoes, and be prepared for some sun exposure, as there is little shade along the way. the trail can be windy, so a light jacket might come in handy. overall, koko crater arch trail offers a unique hiking experience with stunning views that make the effort worthwhile. if you’re up for a bit of a challenge and love scenic vistas, this trail is definitely worth checking out. it is also a pullover sightseeing.

the kwun yum temple is the most famous among the great number of them in the territory. it was built in 1873. in 1909, a road was constructed to connect hung hom with tsim sha tsui and kowloon city. when workers were digging in the hilly areas, red water spouted from the ground. it was rumoured that the vein of the dragon that inhabited in that area had been ruptured as a result of the work. the workers were frightened to continue with the road construction. despite laboratory findings that the colour of the water was due to a mixture of underground deposits of sulphur and mercury, the workers were still worried and donated money to renovate the temple in the belief that kwun yum would be able to help them to avert any subsequent disaster. during the second world war, it was said that hung hom district was under bombardments, aiming at destroying the whampoa dock. there were heavy casualties in the adjacent school but those people taking shelter in the temple were unharmed. the residents in the area believed that it was a miracle of kwun yum. kwun yum or kwun sai yum (觀世音) is known for centuries as a deity of sympathy, compassion and mercy, hearing the pleas of those who are suffering. she is worshipped by people of both the taoist and buddhist religions. kwun yum in the earlier times was a male divinity, but evolved to be a female deity in tang dynasty (唐朝). arising from a saying that kwun yum studied taoist teachings on lotus blossoms, some kwun yum temples are also called lin fa kung or palace of lotus flower (蓮花宮). temples dedicated to kwun yum are often alternatively known as shui yuet kung or palace of water and moon (水月宮), which stands for all that is quiet and peaceful and detached from the material world. architecturally, the temple is a traditional chinese temple. the front hall is shaped like a chinese pavilion. the middle hall looks like a covered-year and the rear part is the main hall where the images of the deities are placed.

the lanikai pillbox hike is an unforgettable experience that’s full of those classic hawai’i vibes with breathtaking ocean views, turquoise waters, and lush greenery everywhere you look. the trail itself isn’t long, it’s a pretty steep incline most of the way up, and definitely not an easy stroll. it’s best for those who are comfortable with hiking and can stably walk and climb. there’s no wheelchair or stroller access, so it’s not the right trail for everyone. parking can be a bit of a challenge since there’s no official lot. most people end up parking in the nearby residential areas or even down by lanikai beach, which means a bit of a walk uphill before you even start the hike. just be super mindful of the local neighborhood but don’t block driveways and respect the homes around you. overall highly recommended this hike if you are able! that said, once you make it to the top, the views are absolutely worth it. you’ll get a stunning panoramic look at the ocean, the mokulua islands, and the coastline below. it’s one of those hikes where the reward totally matches the effort, and the scenery at the top feels like a postcard brought to life.

the le map marrakech - monde des arts de la parure museum is a unique cultural gem located in the heart of the kasbah district of marrakech. it showcases an extraordinary collection of jewelry, adornments, and ceremonial garments from over 50 countries, offering visitors a journey through the rich and diverse artistic traditions of different civilizations. the museum houses approximately 3,000 carefully curated pieces, selected from a remarkable collection of 7,000 items gathered over decades by swiss collectors marlène and paolo bongi-gallon. each piece tells a story of craftsmanship, heritage, and the timeless beauty of decorative arts. the architectural design of le map itself is a masterpiece, featuring an octagonal light well that bathes the interiors in a warm, natural glow. the three-floor structure, covering around 1,400 square meters, is thoughtfully arranged around this central well, creating an intimate yet grand exhibition space. on the upper floor, visitors will find a suspended garden hosting le shams restaurant, where they can enjoy homemade local delicacies while taking in breathtaking views of the old city, the atlas mountains, and the nesting storks—symbols of peace in moroccan culture. reaching the museum is simple. from the famous jemaa el-fnaa square, visitors can walk towards place des ferblantiers, then follow rue ksibat nhas, where clear signs lead the way to the entrance. nearby, bicycle parking is available, and most alsa bus lines provide convenient access to the medina. le map is open from tuesday to sunday, from 10 am to 6 pm, with the last entry at 5:15 pm. as part of its commitment to cultural exchange and artistic appreciation, the museum offers free admission to moroccan students every saturday, fostering a deeper connection between young generations and the world of adornment arts.

the legendary sea stacks of the faroe islands. risin og kellingin (meaning "the giant and the witch" in faroese) are two iconic sea stacks located off the northern coast of eysturoy in the faroe islands. these dramatic basalt formations are steeped in folklore and offer breathtaking views for visitors. visit during summer for milder weather, but fog and storms can add to the mystical atmosphere. risin (the giant): 71–81 meters tall, standing further out to sea. kellingin (the witch): 68–69 meters tall, with a distinctive split shape resembling legs. geologists predict kellingin may collapse within decades due to erosion. according to faroese folklore, these stacks were once an icelandic giant and witch sent to steal the faroe islands. the witch climbed eiðiskollur cliff to tie the islands together, but the mountain cracked, and at sunrise, both were turned to stone. tjørnuvík (streymoy): offers a classic view with a black sand beach foreground. kalsoy & slættaratindur has panoramic vistas from neighboring islands and peaks. the stacks symbolize resilience and are a beloved part of faroese identity, featured on stamps and in local art.

the lion's gate is one of the seven open gates of the old city of jerusalem and leads into the muslim quarter. the start of via dolorosa begins here. legend has it that sultan selim i dreamed of lions that were going to eat him because of his plans to level the city. he was spared only after promising to protect the city by building a wall around it. this led to the lion becoming the heraldic symbol of jerusalem.

the location in the western serengeti was great! it didn't take long to drive to see the migrating herds of wildebeest. this is a larger camp and i'm not such a fan of that. the dinner service was only a buffet. it seems like a lot of money for a buffet and the dinner had limited options (usually some indian dishes, pasta, and then some meat/veggies). breakfast had made-to-order eggs and then the rest was buffet. the lunch boxes were the same thing everyday and not really great (sandwich, fruit, peanuts, water, juice....pretty boring). i stayed in the tented chalet. meh, it's not really a tent. it is quite large. it was clean. there is a flush toilet and shower continuously has hot water. pretty good water pressure and was super hot. towels were nice and fluffy and replaced daily. bed was rock hard. it was super uncomfortable. first night i had trouble sleeping. second was a bit better. there is a single plug for charging devices. the room has poor air circulation and you can't open all the tent window flaps because there were lights from the main building 24/7. wifi was only in the main reception and restaurant and was decent strength, but couldn't do video chat. there was zero cell service at this camp. one other negative is that the restaurant is a .3 km walk from the main reception. overall, it's not a place i'll return to. i really prefer smaller tented camps and for this kind of money i don't expect buffet food.

the location is excellent and the tents are spacious and nicely set up, that’s where the positives end. service was consistently underwhelming. laundry came back wet, staff rarely checked in or offered drinks despite being around all day, and the breakfast buffet was cleared while we were still eating. most of the day, the team seemed disengaged. the food offering is entirely indian cuisine, tasty, but i expected more variety for a multi-day stay. in-room amenities also disappointed: the fan provided couldn’t be used due to the wrong plug. the game drives were scenic, but lacked any real depth. the guide mostly drove silently from one animal to the next while on his phone. there was little context, no storytelling, it felt more like visiting a zoo than exploring an ecosystem. i ended the safari early. also, be aware: lions roam the property at night. while security is present, it’s unnerving, something i wish had been communicated in advance. for the price (including game drives and transfers), i can’t say it delivered the experience i was hoping for.

the location is stunning, and the unit is beautifully appointed and cozy. it had everything we needed for a comfortable and enjoyable stay. we especially appreciated the peaceful surroundings and the thoughtful attention to detail throughout.

the location is truly incredible and magical. the staff is really welcoming and caring ; the reception room is amazing. the food was delicious and so was the tea. however, we had a tent that couldn't lock, and a tourist randomly entered in the tent at 5 am, so we were really scared and confused about that. also the wind kept opening the door and our windows weren't really wind-proof. therefore it was super cold at night. it would've been nicer if the blankets were a little bit thicker. but overall it was an amazing experience.

the location of nayra alto atacama is truly breathtaking, nestled among striking red rocks and a scenic riverbed, just a short drive from san pedro. the setting exudes tranquility and serenity, making it a potentially perfect retreat. however, the hotel clearly needs some refurbishments. the rooms are somewhat dark with dated furniture, and the air conditioning is notably loud and cannot be turned off. the hotel grounds are a delight, featuring an array of cacti, blooming flowers, fruit trees, and even llamas and a vegetable garden. yet, these beautiful features would shine even more with better upkeep and more attentive gardening. the pool area has the potential to be a paradise with its numerous pools; however, with only one heated option, the enjoyment of the others is limited by their chilly temperatures. the spa and thermal baths also need attention, as they appear outdated and not well-maintained. while the staff is friendly and welcoming, the service lacks a polished touch; for instance, don't expect proactive service at the pool area, such as the offer of drinks or the clearing of towels. while i didn't experience the tours personally, they seem varied and led by knowledgeable guides. the food is decent, yet the dining atmosphere could be enhanced to match the overall potential of the hotel. given its current state, the hotel may not meet the expectations set by its pricing or its reputation as a leading hotel of the world.

the location of this hotel is absolutely spectacular. the view from the hotel room was just amazing! we took a bus from el calafate to puerto natales and wanted to drive straight to the hotel which is about 1 1/5 hour drive from natales bus stop. to avoid unnecessary problems and delays, i had coordinated a transfer from and to puerto natales bus stop with the hotel. the hotel driver was waiting at the bus stop. we visited milodon caves on our way to the hotel (for which we had to pay extra 50 usd - though the caves are just on the road and not extra drive would be necessary. i presume we had to pay for the waiting time). the drive was otherwise perfect. after reaching the hotel we checked in and the stay from there on was just amazing. as already mentioned the location is spectacular, there are interesting and beautiful walks around the hotel. breakfast was good. the hotel restaurant is also very good and offers many options - also vegetarian. hotel also offers many activities like horse rides, trekking etc. activities are very good, and like everything else in patagoina very expensive. it is still worth the money - if you can afford it. the reception staff is very friendly and happy to inform about all the activities available - many activities depend on the weather, and it's better to book them at short notice. we were happy we decided to stay at this hotel instead of staying in puerto natales in spite of this option being a more expensive. it saved us a lot of time, and we enjoyed the stunning location. we visited this great hotel in december 2024.

the location on gam island is breathtaking with a gorgeous rainforest and reef. the accommodation is all over water bungalows and the aesthetics are great. you can literally swim off your balcony right onto the reef. the staff is extremely friendly, takes care of anything needed, and even tries to learn everybody’s names. english levels vary, but everybody speaks enough to be functional in their role. diving is unbelievable, really fantastic, and the equipment for rentals was nice. dive team was very professional. food is a mix of western and eastern and veggie/salad options. generally the food was really good, but a few days it was not so good. i recommend diving the following: 1. mayhem: amazing sea creatures, good corals, neat topography, saw numerous wobbegong! 2. melissa’s garden: everybody agreed, this spot has the best coral in the world. it is literally breathtaking how colorful, dense, and diverse the coral is. 3. mioskon: really great corals and a lot of great sea creatures! 4. the viewpoint at piaynemo should not be missed. one of the best views i have ever seen in my life. **there are 4 resident palm cockatoo birds on the resort!! be on the lookout for them as they are amazing looking but a bit challenging to find! also loved the fact that you can snorkel, kayak, or paddle board on the house reef any time for free (unguided). just standing on the jetty my wife and i saw a squid, 4 black tip sharks, a cuddlefish, a walking shark, multiple eels, beautiful parrot fish, and tons of other stuff. negatives/ fyis 1. manta season this year has ended early and so nearly guaranteed sightings in january/february became more like 30% chance viewings by mid march. i was fortunate to see them, but level set expectations as many did not even though online it says the manta season lasts through april. 2. the bird of paradise excursions will not occur if there is rain either right before or during the excursion. in a place where it rains nearly every day, this meant i was able to see wilson’s bird of paradise, but not the red bird of paradise. side note: wilson’s bird of paradise is only located in west papua and absolutely amazing to see!

the location on the nile is beautiful, but if you’re looking for a true five-star place, this isn’t it. almost all the music is gulf, with very few egyptian songs, and most of the guests are gulf visitors. the place itself feels suffocating from all the shisha smoke. the music and sound quality were terrible — it felt like listening to a noisy cassette where you can’t even understand the words. i’m giving a low rating for one main reason: the dancer spent over half an hour going from table to table collecting tips instead of performing. definitely not the level i expected.

the location was absolutely fantastic — we truly loved it. it was incredibly convenient to access the ski slopes right from where we were staying, which made the whole experience seamless and stress-free. the staff were also friendly and helpful, adding to the overall positive vibe of the trip. one of the highlights was the bus transfer to the resort — it was smooth, comfortable, and we had the entire bus to ourselves, which made the journey feel even more special and relaxing. unfortunately, we did fall ill on the last day of our holiday, which put a slight damper on things. it was a shame to end such a great trip on that note, but up until then, everything had been near perfect. overall, we had a wonderful time and would definitely consider returning. and a big shout out to kevin, our amazing ski instructor — you made the trip unforgettable he deserves a raise!

the location was fantastic—right next to the little bridge attraction, with opportunities for some climbing nearby. the cave dining area added a unique and cozy touch to the experience. dinner was chicken rice, and a fresh salad. however, breakfast was quite simple and a little underwhelming. a bit more variety would have been nice. one downside was the shower situation in the ladies’ bathroom, as only one cubicle had hot water, and it was either burning hot or freezing cold. overall, a great spot with a unique setting, but breakfast and shower facilities could use some improvement.

the location was great. the price was great. but the massage with lucia was incredible. she is a true professional and she addressed my minor back injury with great care. i would use lucia again because she is on top of the massage game. strong hands coupled with a head to toes sequence that was second to none. if you make it to this establishment make sure you seek out lucia. she is truly one of the best i've had and i have traveled the world. enjoy!

the lodge is absolutely stunning. the attention to detail in the design and decor is evident, and we instantly felt a sense of luxury and comfort. the accommodations are spacious, well-appointed, and offer breathtaking views of the surrounding wilderness. one of the highlights of our stay was undoubtedly the elephants and the hippopotamus in the front yard of our tent. it was a truly remarkable experience to have such close encounters with these majestic animals. the meals at the camp were thoughtfully prepared and absolutely delicious. we savored every bite and appreciated the variety of culinary delights offered. however, it was the breakfasts in the wild that truly stood out. enjoying breakfast while surrounded by the untamed beauty of nature was an experience that will forever be etched in our memories. our guide, rapz, deserves special recognition. he expertly tracked down lions, elephants, wild dogs, rhinos, and leopards for us, creating unforgettable wildlife encounters. his knowledge and passion for the wildlife were truly inspiring. the locations for breakfast in the middle of the wilderness were breathtaking, and the boat trip through the okavango delta was an experience that will remain etched in our hearts forever. thank you, rapz, for your care and for providing us with such amazing experiences.
